name: Viking Age Scandinavia
title: Social Hierarchy of the Vikings: From Kings to Thralls

tiers.name: Kings
tiers.you: You lead your warriors and reward them with gifts, and the assembly acclaims you, but your own son may rise against you, and you may die in battle.
tiers.kid: Viking kings led armies and fleets, gave gifts to their warriors and in time made their people Christian.
tiers.rise: Kings came from royal families, but no fixed rule of succession existed: sons and kinsmen competed, and the throne went to whoever could win over the chieftains and the assemblies and win the battles.
tiers.why: Kingship in Scandinavia began small: around 800 Norway alone had some 30 petty kingdoms, and kings’ names are reliably known only for the later Viking Age.

tiers.name: Jarls
tiers.you: You hold great estates and a hall full of armed followers and thralls, and you rule a whole region, for a king or in his place.
tiers.kid: Jarls were powerful lords, one step below the king, who owned great farms and ruled whole regions.
tiers.rise: The title passed within great families such as the jarls of Lade and the earls of Orkney, or was granted by a king to a deputy; a jarl who lost a struggle with a king could lose everything, as Håkon Sigurdsson did when Olaf Tryggvason seized Norway in 995.
tiers.why: A jarl (earl) was the greatest lord below a king.

tiers.name: Chieftains
tiers.you: The farmers of your district follow you to the assembly and to war; in return you back them in their lawsuits and hold the feasts at your hall.
tiers.kid: Chieftains led the farmers of their district in war and at the assemblies where laws were made.
tiers.rise: Chieftaincy passed mostly within families, but land, followers and success in feuds and raids could make a rich farmer a chieftain, and in Iceland a goðorð could simply be bought.
tiers.why: Below the jarls stood the chieftains of districts, wealthy landowners who led their neighbours in war and law.

tiers.name: Retainers
tiers.you: You live in your lord’s household, fight at his side and are paid in gifts for your service; if he is killed, you are expected to avenge him.
tiers.kid: Kings and chieftains kept bands of warriors who lived with them and were rewarded with gifts.
tiers.rise: Free men skilled in arms joined a lord’s following by his favour, and loyal service was rewarded with gifts; in Norway the king’s men could rise to be his landed men (lendir menn), the highest rank in the royal household.
tiers.why: Kings, jarls and chieftains kept armed households of free men, called lið and in later sources hirð, who lived with their lord, fought at his side and were rewarded with gifts and pay.

tiers.name: Free farmers
tiers.you: You farm your family’s land with your household, carry your own spear and shield, and stand with the other free men at the thing when laws are made and disputes judged.
tiers.kid: Most Vikings were farmers, not raiders: they grew grain, kept animals and met at assemblies to make laws.
tiers.rise: Sons inherited family land, cleared new land or won wealth abroad; debt, crime or capture in war could reduce a free person to a thrall.
tiers.why: Most free Scandinavians were farmers (bœndr), the karlar of Rígsþula, who worked their own land with their households.

tiers.name: Freed slaves
tiers.you: You have won your freedom, perhaps with a plot of land, but you still owe loyalty to your former owner, who will inherit your farm if you die without children.
tiers.kid: Some thralls were set free, and some were even given land to farm by their former owners.
tiers.rise: Freedom came only by the owner’s choice, by will or by purchase; the freed slave’s grandchildren could expect to count as fully free.
tiers.why: A thrall could be freed by the owner, in the owner’s will, or by buying freedom with money earned; according to the sagas the Norwegian magnate Erling Skjalgsson set each of his thralls a price and let them earn it by…

tiers.name: Thralls
tiers.you: You belong to an owner who can sell you abroad; you herd animals, cut wood and build fences, and you may try to save enough to buy your freedom.
tiers.kid: Thralls were enslaved people, often captured in raids, who were owned by others and made to work without pay.
tiers.rise: Freedom came only through the owner: as a gift, in a will, or by purchase with money the thrall had earned. Slavery faded between the 12th and early 14th centuries, after Scandinavia became Christian.
tiers.why: Thralls were property: they could be bought, sold and punished, and the 12th-century Gulating law made anyone who harmed a thrall pay the owner, as for damage to cattle.
